newsitem.title: USA: Gov. Weld to resign to focus on Mexico envoy bid.
newsitem.headline: Gov. Weld to resign to focus on Mexico envoy bid.

text.p: Republican William Weld will resign as governor of Massachusetts Monday to work full-time for Senate confirmation to be U.S. ambassador to Mexico, an official close to the governor said Sunday.

Weld will hold a press conference at 5 p.m. EDT in Boston on Monday announcing he will resign effective 5 p.m. EDT on Tuesday, at which time Lieutenant Governor Paul Cellucci will become governor, said the source, who declined to be identified.
"He's decided that the business of the state of Massachusetts should not be held up by a confirmation battle in Washington," he said.
Senator Jesse Helms, the North Carolina Republican who heads the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has vowed to block any Senate vote on Weld, whom he deems too soft on drugs for Mexico.

Weld, a rare Republican in a largely Democratic state, has supported the medical use of marijuana and taken abortion and homosexual rights stances that are repulsive to Helms, who has said the governor was below "ambassador quality."
Weld is scheduled to travel to Washington Thursday to begin meetings with top State Department officials, a spokesman said. The governor will also request a meeting with Helms, he said.

When asked if a resignation might cut some leverage the governor enjoyed during the confirmation process, the source said that "even it if makes the nomination more difficult, it's still the right thing to do."
"He's decided it's not right to use the governor's office to lobby for the ambassadorship," he said.
Weld had communicated his decision to resign to White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, said a White House official who declined to be named.

"Governor Weld has been a skilled leader and we continue to believe he will make an excellent ambassador to Mexico," White House spokesman Joe Lockhart told reporters when asked about Weld's reported decison to resign as governor.
The official said Weld made his decision to resign on his own and did not consult the White House on it.

Clinton had hoped that picking Weld, one of the nation's most high-profile Republicans, for a key ambassadorial job would help build a bridge to the Republican leadership in Congress and brush away some of the partisanship complicating his stewardship of foreign affairs.
Senate Majority leader Trent Lott backed away on Sunday from leading a possible charge to rescue Weld's troubled nomination.
"Two weeks ago, we might could have worked out something with the chairman," Lott said, referring to Helms.
"But the biggest problem right now is Governor Weld shot his foot off," Lott said on the NBC programme "Meet the Press."
Earlier this month, Weld called a press conference to challenged the President to fight for the nomination and said his difference with Helms reflect an idealogical rift in the Republican Party.
"In plain language, I am not Sen. Helms's kind of Republican," Weld said.
Lott said of Weld's prospects to win the nomination that, "you never say something is dead in Washington."
But he added, "I don't think his chances are very good."
Weld has sought other political offices since being reelected to a second four-year term in 1994.
The highly-popular governor flirted with the idea of running for the Republican nomination for president for the 1996 race before backing out.
He challenged Senator John Kerry for his seat but was soundly defeated and has been rumoured to be considered by the Clinton administration for various federal posts since.
